title: ML Modules for Mere Mortals
excerpt: An introduction and explanation to the ML module system
content_html:
I think everyone can agree code needs to be modular. Modularity lets us reason locally about our code no matter how big it grows. However, no one seems to agree on how code should be modular. There are a bunch of different approaches and each new language seems to bring their own spin on it.

Today we’re going to talk about a pretty old spin: ML Modules. ML here stands for Meta Language, as seen in SML and OCaml (and not machine learning). Despite SML first appearing in 1983, ML Modules have not caught on. OCaml is the sole production language you’ll find with an ML module system, and at the height of its popularity it’s niche.

This is a shame because ML modules have a lot to offer. We’re going to talk about what ML modules are and then touch a little on why ML modules are. Who better after all to explain modules, than the guy who doesn’t know what’s in a module ?
…On second thought, don’t answer that.
…I already wrote the blog post.

Modules exist to make our code modular, duh, but what does that mean in practice? I think most programmers have some intuitive sense of modularity:

  • Bundle up related logic as one “thing”
  • Encapsulate invariants
  • Decouple from dependencies

Most languages have a way to do this, and if they don’t, one gets created for them (looking at you JavaScript).

Modules Bundle Functions Link to heading

ML modules achieves this with, you guessed it, the Module. ML modules, however, are a little different from the modules we know and love. To explain their differences, we’ll lean on a made-up Rust-inspired syntax. It will start off looking a little weird and gradually, as we introduce concepts, end up looking really weird (but hopefully more familiar than SML syntax). We’ll start by defining a module with just functions:

mod AModule {
  fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
    a + b
  }

  fn sub(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
    a - b
  }

  // mult, div, etc...
}

AModule bundles together related arithmetic functions as one thing we can reason about. Each function can see every other function in the module. This is useful, but any language with namespaces offers this.

Modules (also) Bundle Types Link to heading

A little more unique is that ML modules will let us put not only function definitions in modules, but also type definitions:

mod Set {
  type Set = Vec<i32>;

  fn new() -> Set {
    vec![]
  }

  fn index_of(this: &Set, ele: &i32) -> Result<usize, usize> {
    this.binary_search(ele)
  }

  fn insert(this: Set, ele: i32) -> Set {
    match index_of(&ele) {
      Ok(_) => {} // we're done the element is already present
      Err(indx) => {
        this.insert(indx, ele);
      }
    }
    this
  }

  fn contains(this: &Set, ele: &i32) -> bool {
    index_of(this, ele).is_ok()
  }

  fn remove(this: Set, ele: &i32) -> Set {
    match index_of(this, ele) {
      Err(_) => {}, // we're done the element is already removed
      Ok(indx) => {
        this.remove(indx)
      }
    }
    this
  }
}

Here we have a Set module with a Set type, which is a sorted Vec<i32>. Our module’s functions can refer to the type definitions much the same way they can refer to their module’s function definitions. Okay but that’s not that crazy, still well within the realm of Rust modules.

The Type of a Module is a Signature Link to heading

Not only can modules contain type definitions. Modules themselves have types. A module type is called a signature (so we don’t get it confused with “normal” types). The signature of our Set module is:

sig FullSetSig {
  type Set = Vec<i32>;

  fn new() -> Set;
  fn index_of(&Set, &i32) -> Result<usize, usize>;
  fn insert(Set, i32) -> Set;
  fn contains(&Set, &i32) -> bool;
  fn remove(&Set, &i32) -> Set
}

A module signature declares every definition of a module alongside its type. This might look similar to the way we define a trait in Rust. That’s because much like traits act as interfaces in Rust, signatures act as interfaces in ML Modules. Modules having signatures is the single most important thing to understand about ML Modules. All the complexity and expressiveness of modules results from them having signatures and the wonderful wacky things that enables.

Signatures Support Encapsulation Link to heading

Signatures resemble the way a C/C++ implementation file conforms to its header. Modules, unlike .cc files, aren’t in a 1:1 relationship with signatures. Our Set module can conform to any signature that it matches. A module matches a signature when it defines every declaration in the signature and they agree on type.

Matching a signature provides Encapsulation , hiding internal details of our module from our public API. Take a look at FullSetSig. Do callers of Set really need to know about index_of? Encapsulation advocates shout a resounding no: index_of is an implementation detail of Set.Set being a Vec<i32> and not integral to our Set API.

We can encapsulate index_of by matching our Set module to a new signature:

sig SetSig {
  type Set = Vec<i32>;

  fn new() -> Set;
  // index_of is missing.
  fn insert(Set, i32) -> Set;
  fn contains(&Set, &i32) -> bool;
  fn remove(&Set, &i32) -> Set
}

SetSig removes index_of, hiding the implementation detail. We can then ascribe our signature to our Set module:

mod Set : SetSig {
    // Our module implementation stays unchanged...
}

Now the rest of our code sees Set as SetSig without index_of. Importantly, our Set module hasn’t changed. index_of is still available inside the module. Ascribing the signature only changes the public view of the module, similar to a private function in Rust.

A module’s definition isn’t the only place we can ascribe a signature. We can also make a “new” module by matching an old module to a new signature. Let’s say we want an InsertOnlySet (never you mind why I need that):

sig InsertOnlySetSig {
  type Set = Vec<i32>;

  fn new() -> Set;
  fn insert(Set, i32) -> Set;
}

We can create that from our Set module purely by matching the signature:

mod InsertOnlySet: InsertOnlySetSig = Set;

Now InsertOnlySet is effectively a whole new module, despite the underlying implementation being shared with Set. This is what’s cool about modules. We can repurpose modules “for free” simply by giving them a different signature. If we want to do this in an OO language, we’d have to add a new interface in our class definitiion. But we can slap one of these bad boys anywhere in our codebase.

Sealed Types Seal Encapsulation Link to heading

Ascribing a signature to a module lets us hide implementation details, but there’s a bit of a glaring hole here. Sure we’ve hidden away index_of, but our module broadcasts to the world that type Set is a Vec<i32>! Set relies on our vector being kept in sorted order, but anybody is free to write a function:

fn whoops() {
    let mut set = Set::new();
    // teehee
    set.extend([3, 2, 1]);
    // 💥
    let uh_oh = Set::insert(set, 1);
    // Now our set is [1, 3, 2, 1]
}

Nothing but a small flesh wound in our encapsulation. Fortunately, ML modules foresaw this problem and provided a solution using signatures.

Much the same way a signature lets us hide functions, it also lets us hide types. ML Modules call this an abstract type. If we update SetSig to be:

sig SetSig {
  type Set;

  fn new() -> Set;
  fn insert(Set, i32) -> Set;
  fn contains(&Set, &i32) -> bool;
  fn remove(&Set, &i32) -> Set
}

Our signature no longer broadcasts that type Set is Vec<i32>. Within the Set module we’re free to use type Set as Vec<i32>, but everywhere outside the module type Set is now some unknown type. Because callers know nothing about our newly abstract Set type, all they can do is pass it to and from the methods provided by the Set module. As long as we keep our underlying Vec<i32> sorted within Set, we know no one else is able to mess with it. They simply don’t know enough about the type!

Module’s Version of Generics Link to heading

Our Set module is nearing perfection, but it still leaves a little to be desired: it only works for i32. Now we could of course write a new module SetU64, SetString, on and on everytime we need one, but c’mon there’s gotta be a better way. This isn’t Go.

Generics is the go-to solution for this problem. Heck we’ve even used it ourselves with Vec<i32>. ML Modules, however, have a more modular solution. You can parameterize a module by another a module.

Info

Parameterized modules are sometimes called functors, but that name is confusing and you can’t make me use it.

Think of a parameterized module as a function that takes a module and returns another module. To make our Set accept any type and not just i32, we parameterize it by a module that provides the type of our Set’s elements:

mod Set: SetSig (sig Elem {
  type T
}) {
  type Set = Vec<Elem.T>;

  fn new() -> Set {
    vec![]
  }

  fn index_of(this: &Set, ele: &Elem.T) -> Result<usize, usize> {
    // ...
  }

  fn insert(this: Set, ele: &Elem.T) -> Set {
    // ...
  }

  fn contains(this: &Set, ele: &Elem.T) -> bool {
    index_of(this, ele).is_ok()
  }

  fn remove(this: Set, ele: &Elem.T) -> Set {
    // ...
  }
}

Our newly parameterized Set accepts any module that conforms to Elem. Any module can match Elem as long as it has at least a T definition.

A Teensy Problem Link to heading

With that our Set module supports any type. Except for one teensy detail. I’ve deceived you with some tactical // ...s. If we actually try to implement index_of, we quickly encounter a problem:

fn index_of(this: &Set, ele: &Elem.T) -> Result<usize, usize> {
  this.binary_search_by(|a| ele ??? a)
}

We don’t know how to compare T’s. Rust’s Ord would solve this, of course, but ML modules have modules not traits. Set doesn’t take in just a type, however, it takes in a full module. If we need to know how to compare T’s, we can just ask our Elem module:

mod Set: SetSig (sig Elem {
  type T;
  fn cmp(&T, &T) -> Ordering;
}) {
  // ...
}

Now it’s clear how to implement index_of:

fn index_of(this: &Set, ele: &Elem.T) -> Result<usize, usize> {
  this.binary_search_by(|a| Elem::cmp(ele, a))
}

With our parameterized module implemented, we can create new Set modules by applying them to new argument modules:

mod SetU32 = Set(mod U32 {
  type T = u32;
  fn cmp(a: &T, b: &T) { a < b }
});

SetU32.Set is a Vec<u32> and provides an interface that takes and returns u32 instead of i32. We can do it again as easy as:

mod SetString = Set(mod String {
  type T = String;
  fn cmp(a: &T, b: &T) { /* lexographic ordering probably... */ }
});

Just like that, a whole new module. This time a set of Strings. I could do this all day.

Because we accept a module, we can request anything a module can hold (even a whole other submodule or parameterized module!). The downside is that we have to specify the whole module every time. We have to specify cmp every time we apply our Set module. Rust traits let us write Ord for a type once and use it everywhere implicitly.

Include Keeps Modules Small Link to heading

In practice, we don’t actually repeat how to order our type every time we want a Set. Recall that a signature will match any module that provides what it needs. If we make a big module called U64:

mod U64 {
  type T = u64;

  fn cmp(a: &u64, b: &u64) { a < b }

  fn add(a: u64, b: u64) -> u64 { a + b }
  fn sub(a: u64, b: u64) -> u64 { a - b }
  // ...
}

Then we can use that as our argument to Set:

mod SetU64 = Set(U64);

But hang on, we got into this whole Module business to break up our code. Now we’ve got to dump everything into one module just in case we need it later? That’s not very cash modular of us.

ML modules have a final feature to get us the best of both worlds: include. include expands a module inline within another module. We’re free to split up our U64 module into various submodules: U64Order, U64Arithmetic, etc. Our final U64 module only has to include these submodules:

mod U64 {
  type T = u64;

  include U64Order;
  include U64Arithmetic;
  // ...
}

Modules can be organized into logical components and then combined later to provide convenience (wow!). We’re free to cut up and reassemble modules at the whims’ of the wind. We can even apply a module and include it inline:

mod ABunchOfSetForSomeReason {
  mod SetU64 = Set(U64);
  include SetU64;

  mod SetString = Set(String);
  include SetString;
}

Why do you need one module that’s a bunch of overlapping Sets? I don’t know! I’m not your supervisor. Either way, modules will happily let you do it.

Putting It All Together Link to heading

We’ve covered the basics of modules. Let’s take a look at a more involved examples to get a sense of what modules can offer. We’re gonna use modules to assemble a little build executor. Out build step will be a parameterized module:

mod BuildStep(sig Env {
  mod Cache: CacheSig;
  mod Runner: RunnerSig;
}) {
  // ...
}

Where CacheSig represents a cache of build steps and RunnerSig represents running some command:

sig CacheSig {
  fn is_cached(inputs: &[String], output: &Path) -> bool;
  fn store(inputes: &[String], output: &Path);
}

sig RunnerSig {
  fn run(inputs: &[String], output: &Path);
}

For brevity we’ll keep these pretty simple, but hopefully you can imagine how these might expand. We can then implement BuildSet in terms of our input modules:

mod BuildSet(...) {
  fn run_cached(inputs: &[String], output: &Path) {
    if !Env::Cache::is_cached(inputs, output) {
      Env::Runner::run(inputs, output);
      Env::Cache::store(inputs, output);
    }
  }

  fn compile(src: String) -> String {
    let obj = PathBuf::from(format!("{src}.o"));
    run_cached(&[src], &obj);
    obj.display().to_string()
  }

  fn build(srcs: &[String], output: &Path) {
    let objs: Vec<String> = srcs.iter().map(compile).collect();
    run_cached(objs, output)
  }
}

Our build functions takes a list of source files, compiles them, and then links the object files into a final binary. How does run tell when it’s compiling and when it’s linking? Don’t worry about it! Now that we’ve set that up we can toggle the functionality of our build by controlling what modules we pass to BuildStep. For a real build, we’ll want something like an in-memory cache:

mod MemCache {
  // Pretend this works without locking for multithreading
  static ENTRIES: Vec<(Vec<String>, PathBuf)> = vec![];

  fn is_cached(inputs: &[String], output: &Path) {
    ENTRIES.iter().any(|(cached_inputs, cached_outputs)| {
      inputs == cached_inputs && output == cached_outputs
    })
  }

  fn store(inputs: &[String], output: &Path) {
    ENTRIES.push((inputs.to_vec(), PathBuf::from(output)))
  }
}

Next we’ll want something that runs our commands:

mod ShellRunner {
  fn run(inputs: &[String], output: &Path) {
    let cmd = // magically pick between `cc` and `lld`;
    let output = format!("-o {}", output.display());
    Command::new(cmd)
      .args(inputs)
      .args(output)
      .output()
      .expect("All our commands work first try");
  }
}

We can then assemble our build system via:

mod CachedBuild = BuildStep(mod Env {
  mod Cache = MemCache;
  mod Runner = ShellRunner;
});

But maybe we don’t always want caching. Maybe we want a build that always reruns actions for local testing. We simply swap out our cache module:

mod NoCache {
  fn is_cached(inputs: &[String], outputs: &Path) -> bool {
    false
  }

  fn store(inputs: &[String], outputs: &Path) {
    // nothing to do here
  }
}

mod LocalBuild = BuildStep(mod Env {
  mod Cache = NoCache;
  mod Runner = ShellRunner;
});

Our build system works first try. We wouldn’t write the code bad, of course, but just in case we might want to test it. A FakeRunner will let us do just that:

mod FakeRunner() {
  static COMMANDS: Vec<(Vec<String>, PathBuf)> = vec![];

  fn run(inputs: &[String], output: &Path) {
    COMMANDS.push((inputs.to_vec(), PathBuf::from(output)));
  }

  // A test only helper.
  fn contains_command(inputs: &[String], output: &Path) -> bool {
    // ...
  }
}

Because FakeRunner is a parameterize module, we can create a new module (and a new empty COMMANDS) every time we apply it:

mod Tests {
  mod TestRunner = FakeRunner();
  mod TestBuild = BuildStep(mod Env {
    mod Cache = MemCache;
    mod Runner = TestRunner
  });

  // Write tests against TestBuild using `TestRunner::contains_command`...
}

If we want to check that caching works we can extend our tests with a new fake runner and compare their commands:

mod Tests {
  // TestBuild setup...

  mod UncachedTestRunner = FakeRunner();
  mod UncachedTestBuild = BuildStep(mod Env {
    mod Cache = NoCache;
    mod Runner = UncachedTestRunner;
  })

  // Compare the results of `TestRunner::contains_command` and `UncachedTestRunner::contains_command`...
}

This isn’t earth shattering stuff. If we wanted to replicate this setup in an OO language, however, we would need runtime objects or, heaven forbid, a DI framework. Here we can do it all by wiring up modules statically.

Hopefully this has helped you see what’s cool about modules. Module’s power lies in their signatures. What would require a newtype wrapper or a visibility change in other languages can be accomplished by simply changing the signature a module is viewed at.

With abstract types, this allows for constructing webs of encapsulation where each piece knows precisely what it needs to about its neighbor and no more. Signatures act as this encapsulation boundary, freeing us to reason about our code modularly. As long as our module conforms to the expected signature we can contort and refactor it to our wildest whims and trust that it will continue to integrate into our system as expected. ML Modules are neat and I think they deserve more love and exploration in programming languages.

The downside is that we have to specify the whole module every time. We have to specify cmp every time we apply our Set module. Recall that a signature will match any module that provides what it needs. We can even apply a module and include it inline:mod ABunchOfSetForSomeReason { mod SetU64 = Set(U64); include SetU64; mod SetString = Set(String); include SetString; } Why do you need one module that’s a bunch of overlapping Sets? Let’s take a look at a more involved examples to get a sense of what modules can offer. We’re gonna use modules to assemble a little build executor. Out build step will be a parameterized module:mod BuildStep(sig Env { mod Cache: CacheSig; mod Runner: RunnerSig; }) { // ... } Where CacheSig represents a cache of build steps and RunnerSig represents running some command:sig CacheSig { fn is_cached(inputs: &[String], output: &Path) -> bool; fn store(inputes: &[String], output: &Path); } sig RunnerSig { fn run(inputs: &[String], output: &Path); } For brevity we’ll keep these pretty simple, but hopefully you can imagine how these might expand. We can then implement BuildSet in terms of our input modules:mod BuildSet(...) { fn run_cached(inputs: &[String], output: &Path) { if !Env::Cache::is_cached(inputs, output) { Env::Runner::run(inputs, output); Env::Cache::store(inputs, output); } } fn compile(src: String) -> String { let obj = PathBuf::from(format!("{src}.o")); run_cached(&[src], &obj); obj.display().to_string() } fn build(srcs: &[String], output: &Path) { let objs: Vec<String> = srcs.iter().map(compile).collect(); run_cached(objs, output) } } Our build functions takes a list of source files, compiles them, and then links the object files into a final binary. How does run tell when it’s compiling and when it’s linking? Don’t worry about it! Now that we’ve set that up we can toggle the functionality of our build by controlling what modules we pass to BuildStep. Maybe we want a build that always reruns actions for local testing. We simply swap out our cache module:mod NoCache { fn is_cached(inputs: &[String], outputs: &Path) -> bool { false } fn store(inputs: &[String], outputs: &Path) { // nothing to do here } } mod LocalBuild = BuildStep(mod Env { mod Cache = NoCache; mod Runner = ShellRunner; }); Our build system works first try. We wouldn’t write the code bad, of course, but just in case we might want to test it. A FakeRunner will let us do just that:mod FakeRunner() { static COMMANDS: Vec<(Vec<String>, PathBuf)> = vec![]; fn run(inputs: &[String], output: &Path) { COMMANDS.push((inputs.to_vec(), PathBuf::from(output))); } // A test only helper. fn contains_command(inputs: &[String], output: &Path) -> bool { // ... } } Because FakeRunner is a parameterize module, we can create a new module (and a new empty COMMANDS) every time we apply it:mod Tests { mod TestRunner = FakeRunner(); mod TestBuild = BuildStep(mod Env { mod Cache = MemCache; mod Runner = TestRunner }); // Write tests against TestBuild using `TestRunner::contains_command`... } If we want to check that caching works we can extend our tests with a new fake runner and compare their commands:mod Tests { // TestBuild setup... mod UncachedTestRunner = FakeRunner(); mod UncachedTestBuild = BuildStep(mod Env { mod Cache = NoCache; mod Runner = UncachedTestRunner; }) // Compare the results of `TestRunner::contains_command` and `UncachedTestRunner::contains_command`... } This isn’t earth shattering stuff. If we wanted to replicate this setup in an OO language, however, we would need runtime objects or, heaven forbid, a DI framework. Here we can do it all by wiring up modules statically.Hopefully this has helped you see what’s cool about modules. Module’s power lies in their signatures. What would require a newtype wrapper or a visibility change in other languages can be accomplished by simply changing the signature a module is viewed at.With abstract types, this allows for constructing webs of encapsulation where each piece knows precisely what it needs to about its neighbor and no more. Signatures act as this encapsulation boundary, freeing us to reason about our code modularly. As long as our module conforms to the expected signature we can contort and refactor it to our wildest whims and trust that it will continue to integrate into our system as expected. ML Modules are neat and I think they deserve more love and exploration in programming languages.

content_html_zh:
I think everyone can agree code needs to be modular. Modularity lets us reason locally about our code no matter how big it grows. However, no one seems to agree on how code should be modular. There are a bunch of different approaches and each new language seems to bring their own spin on it.

Today we’re going to talk about a pretty old spin: ML Modules. ML here stands for Meta Language, as seen in SML and OCaml (and not machine learning). Despite SML first appearing in 1983, ML Modules have not caught on. OCaml is the sole production language you’ll find with an ML module system, and at the height of its popularity it’s niche.

This is a shame because ML modules have a lot to offer. We’re going to talk about what ML modules are and then touch a little on why ML modules are. Who better after all to explain modules, than the guy who doesn’t know what’s in a module ?…On second thought, don’t answer that.…I already wrote the blog post.

Modules exist to make our code modular, duh, but what does that mean in practice? I think most programmers have some intuitive sense of modularity:

  • Bundle up related logic as one “thing”
  • Encapsulate invariants
  • Decouple from dependencies

Most languages have a way to do this, and if they don’t, one gets created for them (looking at you JavaScript).

Modules Bundle Functions Link to heading

ML modules achieves this with, you guessed it, the Module. ML modules, however, are a little different from the modules we know and love. To explain their differences, we’ll lean on a made-up Rust-inspired syntax. It will start off looking a little weird and gradually, as we introduce concepts, end up looking really weird (but hopefully more familiar than SML syntax). We’ll start by defining a module with just functions:

mod AModule {
  fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
    a + b
  }

  fn sub(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
    a - b
  }

  // mult, div, etc...
}

AModule bundles together related arithmetic functions as one thing we can reason about. Each function can see every other function in the module. This is useful, but any language with namespaces offers this.

Modules (also) Bundle Types Link to heading

A little more unique is that ML modules will let us put not only function definitions in modules, but also type definitions:

mod Set {
  type Set = Vec<i32>;

  fn new() -> Set {
    vec![]
  }

  fn index_of(this: &Set, ele: &i32) -> Result<usize, usize> {
    this.binary_search(ele)
  }

  fn insert(this: Set, ele: i32) -> Set {
    match index_of(&ele) {
      Ok(_) => {} // we're done the element is already present
      Err(indx) => {
        this.insert(indx, ele);
      }
    }
    this
  }

  fn contains(this: &Set, ele: &i32) -> bool {
    index_of(this, ele).is_ok()
  }

  fn remove(this: Set, ele: &i32) -> Set {
    match index_of(this, ele) {
      Err(_) => {}, // we're done the element is already removed
      Ok(indx) => {
        this.remove(indx)
      }
    }
    this
  }
}

Here we have a Set module with a Set type, which is a sorted Vec<i32>. Our module’s functions can refer to the type definitions much the same way they can refer to their module’s function definitions. Okay but that’s not that crazy, still well within the realm of Rust modules.

The Type of a Module is a Signature Link to heading

Not only can modules contain type definitions. Modules themselves have types. A module type is called a signature (so we don’t get it confused with “normal” types). The signature of our Set module is:

sig FullSetSig {
  type Set = Vec<i32>;

  fn new() -> Set;
  fn index_of(&Set, &i32) -> Result<usize, usize>;
  fn insert(Set, i32) -> Set;
  fn contains(&Set, &i32) -> bool;
  fn remove(&Set, &i32) -> Set
}

A module signature declares every definition of a module alongside its type. This might look similar to the way we define a trait in Rust. That’s because much like traits act as interfaces in Rust, signatures act as interfaces in ML Modules. Modules having signatures is the single most important thing to understand about ML Modules. All the complexity and expressiveness of modules results from them having signatures and the wonderful wacky things that enables.

Signatures Support Encapsulation Link to heading

Signatures resemble the way a C/C++ implementation file conforms to its header. Modules, unlike .cc files, aren’t in a 1:1 relationship with signatures. Our Set module can conform to any signature that it matches. A module matches a signature when it defines every declaration in the signature and they agree on type.

Matching a signature provides Encapsulation , hiding internal details of our module from our public API. Take a look at FullSetSig. Do callers of Set really need to know about index_of? Encapsulation advocates shout a resounding no: index_of is an implementation detail of Set.Set being a Vec<i32> and not integral to our Set API.

We can encapsulate index_of by matching our Set module to a new signature:

sig SetSig {
  type Set = Vec<i32>;

  fn new() -> Set;
  // index_of is missing.
  fn insert(Set, i32) -> Set;
  fn contains(&Set, &i32) -> bool;
  fn remove(&Set, &i32) -> Set
}

SetSig removes index_of, hiding the implementation detail. We can then ascribe our signature to our Set module:

mod Set : SetSig {
    // Our module implementation stays unchanged...
}

Now the rest of our code sees Set as SetSig without index_of. Importantly, our Set module hasn’t changed. index_of is still available inside the module. Ascribing the signature only changes the public view of the module, similar to a private function in Rust.

A module’s definition isn’t the only place we can ascribe a signature. We can also make a “new” module by matching an old module to a new signature. Let’s say we want an InsertOnlySet (never you mind why I need that):

sig InsertOnlySetSig {
  type Set = Vec<i32>;

  fn new() -> Set;
  fn insert(Set, i32) -> Set;
}

We can create that from our Set module purely by matching the signature:

mod InsertOnlySet: InsertOnlySetSig = Set;

Now InsertOnlySet is effectively a whole new module, despite the underlying implementation being shared with Set. This is what’s cool about modules. We can repurpose modules “for free” simply by giving them a different signature. If we want to do this in an OO language, we’d have to add a new interface in our class definitiion. But we can slap one of these bad boys anywhere in our codebase.

Sealed Types Seal Encapsulation Link to heading

Ascribing a signature to a module lets us hide implementation details, but there’s a bit of a glaring hole here. Sure we’ve hidden away index_of, but our module broadcasts to the world that type Set is a Vec<i32>! Set relies on our vector being kept in sorted order, but anybody is free to write a function:

fn whoops() {
    let mut set = Set::new();
    // teehee
    set.extend([3, 2, 1]);
    // 💥
    let uh_oh = Set::insert(set, 1);
    // Now our set is [1, 3, 2, 1]
}

Nothing but a small flesh wound in our encapsulation. Fortunately, ML modules foresaw this problem and provided a solution using signatures.

Much the same way a signature lets us hide functions, it also lets us hide types. ML Modules call this an abstract type. If we update SetSig to be:

sig SetSig {
  type Set;

  fn new() -> Set;
  fn insert(Set, i32) -> Set;
  fn contains(&Set, &i32) -> bool;
  fn remove(&Set, &i32) -> Set
}

Our signature no longer broadcasts that type Set is Vec<i32>. Within the Set module we’re free to use type Set as Vec<i32>, but everywhere outside the module type Set is now some unknown type. Because callers know nothing about our newly abstract Set type, all they can do is pass it to and from the methods provided by the Set module. As long as we keep our underlying Vec<i32> sorted within Set, we know no one else is able to mess with it. They simply don’t know enough about the type!

Module’s Version of Generics Link to heading

Our Set module is nearing perfection, but it still leaves a little to be desired: it only works for i32. Now we could of course write a new module SetU64, SetString, on and on everytime we need one, but c’mon there’s gotta be a better way. This isn’t Go.

Generics is the go-to solution for this problem. Heck we’ve even used it ourselves with Vec<i32>. ML Modules, however, have a more modular solution. You can parameterize a module by another a module.

Info

Parameterized modules are sometimes called functors, but that name is confusing and you can’t make me use it.

Think of a parameterized module as a function that takes a module and returns another module. To make our Set accept any type and not just i32, we parameterize it by a module that provides the type of our Set’s elements:

mod Set: SetSig (sig Elem {
  type T
}) {
  type Set = Vec<Elem.T>;

  fn new() -> Set {
    vec![]
  }

  fn index_of(this: &Set, ele: &Elem.T) -> Result<usize, usize> {
    // ...
  }

  fn insert(this: Set, ele: &Elem.T) -> Set {
    // ...
  }

  fn contains(this: &Set, ele: &Elem.T) -> bool {
    index_of(this, ele).is_ok()
  }

  fn remove(this: Set, ele: &Elem.T) -> Set {
    // ...
  }
}

Our newly parameterized Set accepts any module that conforms to Elem. Any module can match Elem as long as it has at least a T definition.

A Teensy Problem Link to heading

With that our Set module supports any type. Except for one teensy detail. I’ve deceived you with some tactical // ...s. If we actually try to implement index_of, we quickly encounter a problem:

fn index_of(this: &Set, ele: &Elem.T) -> Result<usize, usize> {
  this.binary_search_by(|a| ele ??? a)
}

We don’t know how to compare T’s. Rust’s Ord would solve this, of course, but ML modules have modules not traits. Set doesn’t take in just a type, however, it takes in a full module. If we need to know how to compare T’s, we can just ask our Elem module:

mod Set: SetSig (sig Elem {
  type T;
  fn cmp(&T, &T) -> Ordering;
}) {
  // ...
}

Now it’s clear how to implement index_of:

fn index_of(this: &Set, ele: &Elem.T) -> Result<usize, usize> {
  this.binary_search_by(|a| Elem::cmp(ele, a))
}

With our parameterized module implemented, we can create new Set modules by applying them to new argument modules:

mod SetU32 = Set(mod U32 {
  type T = u32;
  fn cmp(a: &T, b: &T) { a < b }
});

SetU32.Set is a Vec<u32> and provides an interface that takes and returns u32 instead of i32. We can do it again as easy as:

mod SetString = Set(mod String {
  type T = String;
  fn cmp(a: &T, b: &T) { /* lexographic ordering probably... */ }
});

Just like that, a whole new module. This time a set of Strings. I could do this all day.

Because we accept a module, we can request anything a module can hold (even a whole other submodule or parameterized module!). The downside is that we have to specify the whole module every time. We have to specify cmp every time we apply our Set module. Rust traits let us write Ord for a type once and use it everywhere implicitly.

Include Keeps Modules Small Link to heading

In practice, we don’t actually repeat how to order our type every time we want a Set. Recall that a signature will match any module that provides what it needs. If we make a big module called U64:

mod U64 {
  type T = u64;

  fn cmp(a: &u64, b: &u64) { a < b }

  fn add(a: u64, b: u64) -> u64 { a + b }
  fn sub(a: u64, b: u64) -> u64 { a - b }
  // ...
}

Then we can use that as our argument to Set:

mod SetU64 = Set(U64);

But hang on, we got into this whole Module business to break up our code. Now we’ve got to dump everything into one module just in case we need it later? That’s not very cash modular of us.

ML modules have a final feature to get us the best of both worlds: include. include expands a module inline within another module. We’re free to split up our U64 module into various submodules: U64Order, U64Arithmetic, etc. Our final U64 module only has to include these submodules:

mod U64 {
  type T = u64;

  include U64Order;
  include U64Arithmetic;
  // ...
}

Modules can be organized into logical components and then combined later to provide convenience (wow!). We’re free to cut up and reassemble modules at the whims’ of the wind. We can even apply a module and include it inline:

mod ABunchOfSetForSomeReason {
  mod SetU64 = Set(U64);
  include SetU64;

  mod SetString = Set(String);
  include SetString;
}

Why do you need one module that’s a bunch of overlapping Sets? 我不知道！ I’m not your supervisor. Either way, modules will happily let you do it.

Putting It All Together Link to heading

We’ve covered the basics of modules. Let’s take a look at a more involved examples to get a sense of what modules can offer. We’re gonna use modules to assemble a little build executor. Out build step will be a parameterized module:

mod BuildStep(sig Env {
  mod Cache: CacheSig;
  mod Runner: RunnerSig;
}) {
  // ...
}

Where CacheSig represents a cache of build steps and RunnerSig represents running some command:

sig CacheSig {
  fn is_cached(inputs: &[String], output: &Path) -> bool;
  fn store(inputes: &[String], output: &Path);
}

sig RunnerSig {
  fn run(inputs: &[String], output: &Path);
}

For brevity we’ll keep these pretty simple, but hopefully you can imagine how these might expand. We can then implement BuildSet in terms of our input modules:

mod BuildSet(...) {
  fn run_cached(inputs: &[String], output: &Path) {
    if !Env::Cache::is_cached(inputs, output) {
      Env::Runner::run(inputs, output);
      Env::Cache::store(inputs, output);
    }
  }

  fn compile(src: String) -> String {
    let obj = PathBuf::from(format!("{src}.o"));
    run_cached(&[src], &obj);
    obj.display().to_string()
  }

  fn build(srcs: &[String], output: &Path) {
    let objs: Vec<String> = srcs.iter().map(compile).collect();
    run_cached(objs, output)
  }
}

Our build functions takes a list of source files, compiles them, and then links the object files into a final binary. How does run tell when it’s compiling and when it’s linking? Don’t worry about it! Now that we’ve set that up we can toggle the functionality of our build by controlling what modules we pass to BuildStep. For a real build, we’ll want something like an in-memory cache:

mod MemCache {
  // Pretend this works without locking for multithreading
  static ENTRIES: Vec<(Vec<String>, PathBuf)> = vec![];

  fn is_cached(inputs: &[String], output: &Path) {
    ENTRIES.iter().any(|(cached_inputs, cached_outputs)| {
      inputs == cached_inputs && output == cached_outputs
    })
  }

  fn store(inputs: &[String], output: &Path) {
    ENTRIES.push((inputs.to_vec(), PathBuf::from(output)))
  }
}

Next we’ll want something that runs our commands:

mod ShellRunner {
  fn run(inputs: &[String], output: &Path) {
    let cmd = // magically pick between `cc` and `lld`;
    let output = format!("-o {}", output.display());
    Command::new(cmd)
      .args(inputs)
      .args(output)
      .output()
      .expect("All our commands work first try");
  }
}

We can then assemble our build system via:

mod CachedBuild = BuildStep(mod Env {
  mod Cache = MemCache;
  mod Runner = ShellRunner;
});

But maybe we don’t always want caching. Maybe we want a build that always reruns actions for local testing. We simply swap out our cache module:

mod NoCache {
  fn is_cached(inputs: &[String], outputs: &Path) -> bool {
    false
  }

  fn store(inputs: &[String], outputs: &Path) {
    // nothing to do here
  }
}

mod LocalBuild = BuildStep(mod Env {
  mod Cache = NoCache;
  mod Runner = ShellRunner;
});

Our build system works first try. We wouldn’t write the code bad, of course, but just in case we might want to test it. A FakeRunner will let us do just that:

mod FakeRunner() {
  static COMMANDS: Vec<(Vec<String>, PathBuf)> = vec![];

  fn run(inputs: &[String], output: &Path) {
    COMMANDS.push((inputs.to_vec(), PathBuf::from(output)));
  }

  // A test only helper.
  fn contains_command(inputs: &[String], output: &Path) -> bool {
    // ...
  }
}

Because FakeRunner is a parameterize module, we can create a new module (and a new empty COMMANDS) every time we apply it:

mod Tests {
  mod TestRunner = FakeRunner();
  mod TestBuild = BuildStep(mod Env {
    mod Cache = MemCache;
    mod Runner = TestRunner
  });

  // Write tests against TestBuild using `TestRunner::contains_command`...
}

If we want to check that caching works we can extend our tests with a new fake runner and compare their commands:

mod Tests {
  // TestBuild setup...

  mod UncachedTestRunner = FakeRunner();
  mod UncachedTestBuild = BuildStep(mod Env {
    mod Cache = NoCache;
    mod Runner = UncachedTestRunner;
  })

  // Compare the results of `TestRunner::contains_command` and `UncachedTestRunner::contains_command`...
}

This isn’t earth shattering stuff. If we wanted to replicate this setup in an OO language, however, we would need runtime objects or, heaven forbid, a DI framework. Here we can do it all by wiring up modules statically.

Hopefully this has helped you see what’s cool about modules. Module’s power lies in their signatures. What would require a newtype wrapper or a visibility change in other languages can be accomplished by simply changing the signature a module is viewed at.

With abstract types, this allows for constructing webs of encapsulation where each piece knows precisely what it needs to about its neighbor and no more. Signatures act as this encapsulation boundary, freeing us to reason about our code modularly. As long as our module conforms to the expected signature we can contort and refactor it to our wildest whims and trust that it will continue to integrate into our system as expected. ML Modules are neat and I think they deserve more love and exploration in programming languages.
